questions.explanation: Ehrenwerth reports very low resistance in standard corrugated tubing, below the stated 1 cmH2O/L/min value. This figure refers to the tubing, not total patient airway or circuit resistance.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 103

questions.stem: Gas flow through corrugated breathing tubing is almost always:
options: Laminar at low flow, turbulent only above 30 L/min
questions.explanation: Corrugations promote radial and longitudinal mixing, so flow is described as almost always turbulent. Low resistance in this wide tubing does not imply laminar flow.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 103

questions.stem: Why don't expandable "concertina" extensions significantly add apparatus dead space?
options: They contain a one-way valve that blocks rebreathing
Their bore is larger, so gas passes faster
They add only compliant volume, not true dead space
They lie downstream of the Y-piece
questions.explanation: Tubing on the circuit side of competent unidirectional valves does not become ordinary rebreathed apparatus dead space merely because it is longer. Its compliance and gas compression can still affect delivered volume.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 103

questions.stem: Per the lecture, how is a circuit tested before use?
options: Pressurize to 75 cmH2O and hold for 1 minute
Find the O2 inflow needed to maintain 30 cmH2O in the circuit
Occlude the Y and confirm the bag empties in 5 seconds
Measure tidal volume with the ventilator off
questions.explanation: Ehrenwerth describes checking the oxygen inflow required to maintain circuit pressure at 30 cmH2O. This is a described leak test rather than a complete universal checkout procedure for every workstation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 103

questions.stem: When does the inspiratory unidirectional valve open?
options: Only when the APL (adjustable pressure-limiting valve) is closed
questions.explanation: The inspiratory valve opens during inspiration and closes during expiration. This prevents exhaled gas from moving backward into the inspiratory limb.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 103

questions.stem: What is the only critical requirement for the location of unidirectional valves in a circle?
options: One between the patient and the bag in each limb
Both must be housed inside the absorber canister
Both must be on the patient side of the Y-piece
One must sit between the APL (adjustable pressure-limiting) valve and the scavenger
questions.explanation: One unidirectional valve must lie between the patient and reservoir bag in each limb. Their precise locations may vary while preserving directional flow.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed pp. 103–104

questions.stem: In a properly working circle system, what is the only apparatus dead space?
options: The absorber canister and its housing
The full inspiratory limb from the valve onward
The entire expiratory limb back to the absorber
The distal Y-piece plus anything beyond it
questions.explanation: With competent unidirectional valves, apparatus dead space is limited to the shared pathway at the distal Y-piece and between it and the patient. The separate inspiratory and expiratory limbs do not normally add that shared dead space.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 104

questions.stem: The expiratory valve disc sticks open. What happens?
options: The circuit becomes occluded and peak pressure rises sharply
Nothing changes, since the inspiratory valve stops rebreathing
Exhaled gas is rebreathed, raising inspired CO2
Inspired CO2 falls because more gas reaches the absorber
questions.explanation: An expiratory valve that fails to seal permits reverse flow and rebreathing. This can increase inspired carbon dioxide despite adequate absorbent.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 104

questions.stem: Why must unidirectional valve discs be hydrophobic?
options: So condensation doesn’t stick them to the knife edge
So they don’t absorb volatile agent during long cases
So they repel CO2 molecules away from the valve seat
So they can be steam autoclaved between patients
questions.explanation: Hydrophobic valve disks resist sticking caused by condensed water. Sticking would increase the pressure needed to open the valve and could obstruct gas flow.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 104

questions.stem: The common valves in anesthesia circuits are which type?
options: Electronic solenoid valves controlled by the vent
Rubber duckbill valves that flex open
Spring-loaded ball valves seated in a cage
Dome valves with a light disk on a circular knife edge
questions.explanation: A typical dome valve uses a lightweight rigid disk resting on a circular knife edge. Flow lifts the disk, while reverse pressure helps seat it and prevent backflow.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 104

questions.stem: Inspired CO2 is rising on the capnogram and the absorbent is fresh. Which machine-check item most likely failed?
questions.explanation: A leaking unidirectional valve permits carbon dioxide-containing exhaled gas to return without proper directional passage through the circle. Thus fresh absorbent alone does not exclude valve-related rebreathing.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 104

questions.stem: Which are functions of the reservoir bag? Select 3.
options: Visual check of ventilation and rough volume
Removal of CO2 from exhaled gas
Reservoir of gas the patient can inspire from
questions.explanation: The reservoir bag stores gas for inspiration, permits a rough visual assessment of ventilation, and enables manual ventilation. Bag movement is influenced by fresh gas flow and is not a precise tidal-volume measurement.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 105

questions.stem: Why does a spontaneously breathing patient need a reservoir bag rather than relying on fresh gas flow?
options: The bag removes CO2 before each inspiration
Fresh gas flow pauses during each inspiratory phase
The bag warms and humidifies the inspired gas
Peak inspiratory flow exceeds fresh gas flow
questions.explanation: Peak inspiratory demand can exceed the continuous fresh gas flow. The reservoir supplies the additional gas needed during inspiration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 105

questions.stem: What reservoir bag size suits most adults?
questions.explanation: A 3-L reservoir bag meets the needs of most adults described in Ehrenwerth. It provides capacity for a deep breath while remaining easy to grasp for manual ventilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 105

questions.stem: How should the optimal reservoir bag volume compare with the patient's inspiratory capacity?
options: It should equal the FRC (functional residual capacity)
It should be half the inspiratory capacity
It should exceed the inspiratory capacity
It should equal the tidal volume
questions.explanation: The bag should hold more than the patient’s inspiratory capacity. A spontaneous deep inspiration should not completely empty it.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 105

questions.stem: Bag pressure-volume characteristics matter most in which situation?
options: The bag is smaller than tidal volume
The APL (adjustable pressure-limiting valve) is left closed with gas still flowing in
The O2 flush is never used
The patient is breathing spontaneously with the APL (adjustable pressure-limiting valve) open
questions.explanation: If the APL valve remains closed while gas continues entering, the bag can overdistend and transmit pressure to the patient. Its pressure-volume behavior therefore becomes important in this fault condition.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 106

questions.stem: Where is the preferred fresh gas inflow site in a circle system?
options: Between the APL (adjustable pressure-limiting) valve and the bag
Between the CO2 absorber and the inspiratory valve
Between the expiratory valve and the absorber
questions.explanation: The preferred fresh gas inlet is between the carbon dioxide absorber and inspiratory valve. This supplies fresh gas to the inspiratory side of the circle.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 106

questions.stem: Tightening the APL (adjustable pressure-limiting) valve during spontaneous ventilation has what effect?
options: Increases circuit pressure, adding PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure)
Decreases circuit pressure, removing PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure)
questions.explanation: Tightening the APL increases the pressure required for gas to escape. During spontaneous ventilation this can raise circuit pressure and produce PEEP.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 106

questions.stem: During spontaneous ventilation, the APL (adjustable pressure-limiting valve) is gradually closed. What happens to circuit pressure?
options: Pressure rises as less gas leaves the circuit
Circuit pressure is unchanged; only scavenging changes
Circuit pressure falls; more gas leaves
questions.explanation: Closing the APL reduces venting and raises circuit pressure as gas accumulates. It should not be interpreted as eliminating rebreathing or guaranteeing safe pressure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 106

questions.stem: In Mapleson circuits, what does a pop-off valve do regarding rebreathing?
options: It converts the circuit to a closed system
It prevents rebreathing only during spontaneous breathing
questions.explanation: A pop-off valve vents excess gas but does not itself separate inspired gas from exhaled gas. Rebreathing in a Mapleson system depends on fresh-gas flow, circuit arrangement, and the respiratory pattern.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 114

questions.stem: Mapleson circuits use total fresh gas flows of about:
questions.explanation: The cited description uses total flows of about one to two times minute ventilation. This is a general Mapleson example rather than a guaranteed minimum for every circuit and ventilation pattern.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 114

questions.stem: Where is the pop-off valve most efficiently placed in a Mapleson circuit?
options: At the bag end during every mode, spontaneous or controlled
Right where fresh gas enters the circuit
Where CO2 is highest while circuit pressure is above atmospheric
Wherever CO2 concentration is lowest in the circuit
questions.explanation: Efficient venting removes the most CO2-rich gas when circuit pressure can open the pop-off valve. Venting fresh gas instead wastes flow without removing as much exhaled CO2.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed pp. 114–115

questions.stem: With controlled ventilation, when does the highest CO2 concentration coincide with positive circuit pressure?
questions.explanation: During controlled or manually assisted ventilation, the relevant CO2-rich mixture is expelled while positive pressure is applied during inspiration. This differs from the favorable venting phase during spontaneous breathing.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed pp. 114–115

questions.stem: Which Mapleson circuit is most efficient for spontaneous, unassisted ventilation?
questions.explanation: Mapleson A is the most efficient configuration for spontaneous, unassisted ventilation. Its arrangement preferentially vents carbon dioxide-rich alveolar gas during expiration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 115

questions.stem: The Bain circuit is a coaxial version of which Mapleson type?
questions.explanation: The Bain circuit is a coaxial modification of Mapleson D. Fresh gas travels through the inner tube toward the patient while exhaled gas returns through the outer tubing.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 117

questions.stem: Which Mapleson circuits are most efficient for assisted or controlled ventilation?
questions.explanation: Mapleson D, E, and F are the most efficient groups for assisted or controlled ventilation. Their efficiency depends on matching fresh gas washout to the ventilation pattern.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 115

questions.stem: The Jackson-Rees circuit belongs to which Mapleson group?
questions.explanation: The Jackson-Rees modification is Mapleson F. It adds a bag to the T-piece arrangement to facilitate assisted or controlled ventilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 115

questions.stem: Which component do Mapleson circuits lack compared with a circle system?
questions.explanation: Mapleson circuits lack a carbon dioxide absorber. Carbon dioxide elimination instead depends on fresh gas flow and the arrangement of the circuit components.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 115

questions.stem: How do Mapleson circuits differ from a circle in their limbs?
options: One tube serves both inspiration and expiration
They have no tubing at all
They have separate inspiratory and expiratory limbs
questions.explanation: In the basic Mapleson arrangement, one breathing tube serves both inspiration and expiration. This differs from a circle system with separate inspiratory and expiratory limbs.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 115

questions.stem: On this figure, which numbered circuit is most efficient for spontaneous breathing?
questions.explanation: Circuit 1 has the Mapleson A arrangement, with fresh gas entering near the bag and the pop-off valve near the patient. Mapleson A is the most efficient listed configuration for spontaneous breathing.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 115

questions.stem: Which numbered circuit corresponds to the Bain (coaxial Mapleson D) design?
questions.explanation: Circuit 4 has the Mapleson D arrangement. The Bain circuit is the coaxial version of that layout; the drawing identifies the underlying arrangement rather than showing the inner coaxial tube.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed pp. 115–117

questions.stem: Which numbered circuit has no reservoir bag (a T-piece)?
questions.explanation: Circuit 5 ends in an open expiratory limb and has no reservoir bag, matching Mapleson E. The open limb provides a gas reservoir and allows exhaled gas to leave.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 115

questions.stem: Which numbered circuit is the Jackson-Rees modification with an open-tailed bag?
questions.explanation: Circuit 6 adds an open-tailed reservoir bag to the T-piece arrangement. This is the Jackson-Rees modification, classified as Mapleson F.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed pp. 115–117

questions.stem: In circuit 1, where is fresh gas introduced relative to the pop-off valve?
options: At the bag end, away from the pop-off
At the patient end, next to the pop-off
questions.explanation: In circuit 1, the fresh-gas inlet is next to the reservoir bag. The pop-off valve is at the patient end, so the inlet and valve lie at opposite ends of the tubing.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 115

questions.stem: Which numbered circuit has the bag and pop-off together at the patient end, with no tubing between?
questions.explanation: Circuit 3 has the compact Mapleson C arrangement, with the bag and pop-off valve near the patient. There is no intervening long corrugated tube between those components.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 115

questions.stem: What does a heat and moisture exchanger do?
options: Adds water from a reservoir to inspired gas
Actively heats inspired gas with an electric element
Passively traps exhaled heat and moisture
questions.explanation: An HME passively retains heat and moisture from exhaled gas and returns some during inspiration. It does not actively heat water or absorb carbon dioxide.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed pp. 183–187

questions.stem: What does adding a filter to an HME (heat and moisture exchanger), making it an HMEF, provide?
options: Active heating of the inspired gas
questions.explanation: An HMEF (heat and moisture exchanger with filter) combines heat and moisture exchange with filtration of airborne and waterborne particles. Filtration reduces transmission but does not guarantee complete protection against every pathogen.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed pp. 183–188

questions.stem: Why does an ETT (endotracheal tube) disrupt normal heat and moisture exchange?
options: It bypasses the upper airway, which normally conditions inspired gas
It adds water to the airway
It increases evaporation from the trachea only during exhalation
It cools inspired gas by the Venturi effect
questions.explanation: An endotracheal tube bypasses the upper airway, which normally warms and humidifies inspired gas. Dry medical gas therefore shifts the conditioning burden to more distal airways.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 183

questions.stem: By what point in the airway has most heating and humidification occurred?
questions.explanation: Most airway warming and humidification has occurred by the mid-trachea. Further conditioning continues distally until inspired gas reaches body temperature and full saturation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 184

questions.stem: The isothermic saturation boundary is the point where inspired gas reaches what?
questions.explanation: The isothermic saturation boundary is where inspired gas reaches 37°C and 100% relative humidity. At that point, its absolute humidity is approximately 44 mg/L.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 184

questions.stem: Where does the isothermic saturation boundary normally lie?
questions.explanation: The isothermic saturation boundary usually lies just below the carina. Its location changes with inspired gas temperature, humidity, and volume.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 184

questions.stem: Breathing dry gas through an ETT (endotracheal tube) for hours moves the isothermic saturation boundary in which direction?
options: Into the upper airway above the vocal cords
Distally, exposing smaller airways to injury
questions.explanation: Intubation with dry gases moves the isothermic saturation boundary distally. More distal airway surfaces must then supply heat and water, increasing their exposure to drying.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed pp. 184–185

questions.stem: In a normal adult, the daily net loss from airway conditioning is about:
questions.explanation: Ehrenwerth estimates a typical adult net airway-conditioning loss of approximately 250 mL of water and 250 kcal daily. These are approximate physiologic values rather than exact losses for every patient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 184

questions.stem: The upper airway acts like what type of device?
options: An active heated humidifier with a water reservoir
A chemical absorber that removes inspired CO2
A one-way valve that directs gas to the alveoli
A countercurrent heat and moisture exchanger
questions.explanation: The upper airway functions as a countercurrent heat and moisture exchanger. Exhaled gas returns heat and moisture to mucosa that subsequently conditions inspired gas.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 184

questions.stem: Which regions do most humidification because of their mucous glands?
questions.explanation: The cited text identifies the nose, trachea, and bronchi as major humidifying regions because of their mucus glands. Their moist surfaces transfer water to inspired gas.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 185

questions.stem: Why do the nasopharynx, pharynx, and larynx contribute little to humidification?
options: They are lined with squamous epithelium
They are lined with ciliated columnar epithelium
questions.explanation: The humidification chapter associates squamous epithelium in portions of the pharynx and larynx with relatively limited humidification. Most airway humidification is attributed to mucus-rich respiratory surfaces; epithelial patterns vary by exact anatomical subsite.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 7, printed pp. 185 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Which cells form respiratory mucus in response to tracheal irritation?
questions.explanation: Goblet cells produce respiratory mucus in response to airway irritation. Secreted droplets absorb water and coalesce into the mucus layer associated with the cilia.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 185

questions.stem: Which are consequences of underhumidification? Select 3.
options: Viscous mucus that slows ciliary movement
Inaccurate flow sensor readings from condensation
ETT (endotracheal tube) obstruction from thick secretions
questions.explanation: Dry gas draws water from airway secretions, making mucus more viscous and reducing ciliary clearance. Thick secretions can obstruct the tracheal tube, and respiratory heat loss can worsen hypothermia.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 185

questions.stem: Which are consequences of overhumidification? Select 3.
options: Inaccurate volume readings from water at the flow sensors
Distal shift of the isothermic saturation boundary
questions.explanation: Excess water can condense in the airway and equipment. The cited text lists surfactant dilution, water intoxication, and inaccurate volume readings when water interferes with flow sensors.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed pp. 185–186

questions.stem: Per the instructor, what helps prevent underhumidification during anesthesia?
options: High fresh gas flows of dry medical gas
Cooling inspired gas below body temperature
Removing the HME (heat and moisture exchanger) to lower airway resistance
Low flows that keep rebreathed gas warm and moist
questions.explanation: Lower fresh gas flow increases rebreathing of warm, humid exhaled gas. This conserves airway heat and moisture, although low flow alone may provide less humidification than an HME.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed pp. 187–188

questions.stem: Raising fresh gas flow from 1 L/min to 8 L/min has what effect on inspired humidity and temperature?
options: Both decrease as dry fresh gas replaces rebreathed gas
Both increase, because more gas passes the absorber
questions.explanation: Higher fresh gas flow replaces more warm, humid exhaled gas with dry medical gas. Inspired heat and moisture conservation therefore generally decrease as flow rises, with the exact effect depending on the circuit and humidifier.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed pp. 187–188

questions.stem: HME (heat and moisture exchanger) efficiency is reduced in which situation?
options: Large tidal volumes, especially with membrane models
Use with a cuffed endotracheal tube
Small tidal volumes in adult patients
Low fresh gas flows during long maintenance phases
questions.explanation: HME performance can fall with large tidal volumes, particularly in membrane-based hydrophobic devices. Performance measured in a laboratory may therefore differ from that achieved in an individual patient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 187

questions.stem: A filter with 99.97% efficiency lets about how many test particles through per 100,000?
questions.explanation: A 99.97% filtration efficiency leaves 0.03% of challenge particles unfiltered. Multiplying 100,000 by 0.0003 gives 30 particles; this describes the test conditions rather than guaranteed clinical pathogen removal.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 186

questions.stem: Bacterial and viral filtration efficiency are tested with droplets about what size?
questions.explanation: The described bacterial and viral filtration challenges use organisms aerosolized into droplets around 3.0 µm. This is the challenge-droplet size, not the diameter of an individual virus or the most penetrating particle size.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 186

questions.stem: What is the basic principle of closed-circuit anesthesia?
options: Venting all exhaled gas to the scavenger
Adding gases at the rate the body removes them
Delivering fresh gas at twice minute ventilation
questions.explanation: Closed-circuit anesthesia adds gases at the rate they are removed by patient uptake and other losses. Exhaled gases are reused after carbon dioxide absorption.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed p. 433

questions.stem: How is the anesthetic state established before switching to closed-circuit flows?
options: Low fresh gas flow from the start
Closed circuit from induction with the vaporizer at maximum
High fresh gas flow first, then FGF lowered near steady state
questions.explanation: Higher fresh gas flow establishes the desired circuit and alveolar concentrations more quickly before flow is reduced. Switching to low or closed flow requires continued gas monitoring rather than assuming that inspired and expired concentrations must become identical.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed p. 433

questions.stem: In a fully closed circuit, the O2 flow into the circuit equals what?
questions.explanation: In an ideal leak-free closed circuit, oxygen input matches oxygen consumption. Real circuit leaks and any gas removed by sampling must also be considered when maintaining circuit volume and oxygen concentration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed p. 441

questions.stem: In a closed circuit, O2 administration exceeds O2 uptake. What happens to FiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen)?
questions.explanation: If oxygen enters a truly closed circuit faster than it is removed, oxygen accumulates. The inspired oxygen fraction consequently rises as the circuit composition changes.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed p. 441

questions.stem: In a LOW-flow (not closed) circuit, O2 delivery slightly exceeds uptake. Why can FiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen) still fall?
options: The proportioning system lowers O2 at low flow
The vaporizer consumes O2 as it adds agent
O2 is absorbed by the CO2 absorbent granules
O2 leaves with the excess gas through the APL (adjustable pressure-limiting valve)
questions.explanation: A semiclosed circuit loses oxygen along with gas vented through its outlet. Oxygen delivery only slightly above patient uptake may therefore fail to replace all oxygen losses, allowing inspired oxygen concentration to fall.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed pp. 101–106

questions.stem: Which are advantages of closed-circuit anesthesia? Select 3.
options: O2 consumption can be monitored by titration
No need for inspired and expired gas monitoring
Exhaled gases are already warmed and humidified
Faster changes in anesthetic depth when needed
Elimination of the CO2 absorber from the circuit
questions.explanation: Closed and low-flow techniques conserve exhaled heat and moisture and reduce anesthetic waste. The proposed use of titration to monitor oxygen consumption is supported for controlled closed-system conditions, rather than as a substitute for gas monitoring.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed p. 433

questions.stem: Compared with a semi-closed circuit, inspired and expired gas tensions with a closed circuit are:
questions.explanation: Comparable inspired and expired anesthetic tensions can be achieved with either technique when delivery is adjusted to the same patient targets. This does not mean inspired tension equals expired tension within either circuit.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed pp. 433–435

questions.stem: In the low-flow example, 8 L/min with 5% isoflurane runs for 2 minutes. What is changed next?
options: Both FGF (fresh gas flow) and vaporizer are turned off
The vaporizer is lowered to 1%, leaving FGF at 8 L/min
FGF is lowered to 2 L/min, leaving the vaporizer setting
questions.explanation: In this specific modeled example, fresh-gas flow falls from 8 to 2 L/min after two minutes while the vaporizer initially stays at 5%. Later adjustments follow measured anesthetic tension; this is an illustrative sequence rather than a universal induction protocol.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed pp. 440–441

questions.stem: The low-flow example targets what expired isoflurane concentration as 1 MAC (minimum alveolar concentration)?
questions.explanation: The textbook model uses 1.1% expired isoflurane as its 1-MAC target. That is a model assumption, not an age-independent concentration requirement for every patient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed p. 440

questions.stem: Which circuit is the most commonly used in the world?
options: Fully closed circuit at basal flows
Semi-closed circle with a CO2 absorber
Mapleson A with high fresh gas flow
questions.explanation: The semi-closed circle with absorber.
questions.citation: McPherson, Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 28

questions.stem: FGF (fresh gas flow) is lowered from 8 L/min to 1 L/min while keeping the same inspired agent tension. What must happen to the vaporizer setting?
questions.explanation: With continuing anesthetic uptake, exhaled agent tension is lower than the inspired target. Lowering fresh-gas flow increases the rebreathed fraction, so a higher vaporizer setting is needed to maintain that target under those conditions.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed p. 442

questions.stem: Why does exhaled gas lower inspired agent tension in a semi-closed circuit?
options: Exhaled gas has higher tension than inspired gas
Exhaled gas contains no anesthetic at all
Uptake leaves exhaled gas with lower agent tension
The absorber removes anesthetic from exhaled gas
questions.explanation: Patient uptake leaves exhaled gas with a lower anesthetic concentration than inspired gas while net uptake continues. Mixing that gas with fresh gas reduces the resulting inspired concentration relative to fresh gas output.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 114

questions.stem: Which changes speed the rise in alveolar anesthetic concentration? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Higher delivered concentration and fresh-gas flow can speed circuit wash-in, while greater effective alveolar ventilation can speed transfer into the lungs. These effects depend on uptake and ventilation efficiency rather than minute ventilation alone guaranteeing a fixed response.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed p. 442; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 81

questions.stem: In the instructor's example, sevo is dialed so inspired is 2.3% to achieve expired 2%. Why the difference?
options: Agent is constantly taken up, so inspired must run higher
The analyzer reads inspired gas falsely high
Expired gas is diluted only by apparatus dead space
The vaporizer overdelivers at low fresh gas flow
questions.explanation: In a semi-closed system you add a little more because you are constantly losing some.
questions.citation: McPherson, Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 28

questions.stem: Even in ideal conditions, brain anesthetic level lags end-tidal by about how long?
questions.explanation: The textbook describes a brain equilibration delay of roughly 3–5 minutes even when end-tidal gas closely reflects alveolar and arterial tension. End-tidal changes therefore do not imply an instantaneous change at the effect site.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed pp. 435–436

questions.stem: End-tidal anesthetic concentration is used as an approximation of what?
options: Alveolar, and in turn blood, concentration
Brain concentration, with no time delay
questions.explanation: Expired anesthetic concentration is used as an approximation of alveolar tension and, in turn, arterial blood tension. Physiologic mismatch can weaken these approximations.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed p. 435

questions.stem: Which are used to assess anesthetic depth? Select 3.
questions.explanation: The cited assessment discussion includes pupils, processed EEG when used, and expired anesthetic concentration. Fresh-gas flow or absorbent color alone does not establish anesthetic depth.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed p. 435

questions.stem: After raising the vaporizer, end-tidal agent rises quickly but the patient still moves. What best explains this?
options: Brain tension lags end-tidal by several minutes
High FGF (fresh gas flow) prevents brain uptake
questions.explanation: Brain and spinal-cord anesthetic tension can lag a rapidly changing end-tidal measurement. This delay can contribute to a clinical response persisting briefly after the displayed agent level rises.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed pp. 435–436

questions.stem: Which machine-check finding means unidirectional valves need attention?
options: The bag fills with the APL (adjustable pressure-limiting valve) closed
The APL (adjustable pressure-limiting valve) holds 30 cmH2O
The O2 analyzer reads 21% in room air at baseline
A valve disc fails to seat during the flow test
questions.explanation: A valve disk that fails to seat may permit reverse flow and carbon dioxide rebreathing. Valve competence therefore requires attention even when other parts of the machine checkout appear normal.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 104

questions.stem: A Mapleson D is used for a spontaneously breathing adult at low FGF (fresh gas flow). What happens?
options: Significant rebreathing, since D suits controlled breathing
No rebreathing, since D is efficient in every breathing mode
Barotrauma, since the pop-off sits near the bag
Hypoxia, since O2 is taken up by the absorbent
questions.explanation: Mapleson D is less efficient during spontaneous ventilation than during assisted or controlled ventilation. With insufficient fresh-gas flow, exhaled CO2 is not adequately flushed and rebreathing can occur.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 4, printed pp. 115–117 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Why do Mapleson circuits need higher fresh gas flows than a circle?
options: They have no absorber, so fresh gas must wash out CO2
They have higher resistance to gas flow overall
They lack a dedicated fresh gas inlet
Their reservoir bags are much smaller
questions.explanation: Mapleson circuits lack a CO2 absorber and depend on sufficient fresh-gas flow to wash exhaled CO2 out of the circuit. A circle system can chemically absorb CO2 and therefore supports lower fresh-gas flows.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 4, printed pp. 107, 115 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Total response time of a gas analyzer equals what?
options: Rise time multiplied by respiratory rate
questions.explanation: Total response time is transit time plus analyzer rise time. Transit time is sample travel; rise time is the analyzer's response to a concentration change.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed pp. 195–197

questions.stem: The time for a gas sample to travel from the circuit to the monitor is called:
questions.explanation: Transit time is the delay while a sidestream gas sample travels from the patient circuit to the analyzer.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 195

questions.stem: The time an analyzer takes to react to a change in gas concentration is called:
questions.explanation: Rise time measures how quickly the analyzer responds after gas concentration changes; it is distinct from sample transit time.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed pp. 195–197

questions.stem: Lengthening the sidestream sampling line mainly increases which component of response time?
questions.explanation: A longer sidestream line delays sample arrival and increases transit time. Analyzer rise time is a separate component.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed pp. 195–197

questions.stem: Why does the displayed EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) lag behind what is happening at the airway?
options: The monitor averages 10 minutes of data
Transit and rise time delay the reading
EtCO2 is measured only during inspiration
questions.explanation: Sidestream sampling takes time to reach the analyzer, and the analyzer takes additional time to respond. Both delays make the displayed CO2 change appear later.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed pp. 195–197

questions.stem: Which sampling method places the analyzer directly in the main gas stream?
questions.explanation: Mainstream gas analysis places the sensor interface directly in the main gas stream at the airway. Unlike sidestream analysis, it does not divert gas through a sampling line.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 195, 197 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Mainstream analyzers are also described as:
questions.explanation: Mainstream gas analysis is also called nondiverting analysis because the gas remains in the breathing circuit. Sidestream systems divert a sample through tubing to a remote analyzer.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 195 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Which describe mainstream gas analysis? Select 3.
options: Readings affected by secretions, water vapor, and blood
Gas continuously aspirated to a remote analyzer
questions.explanation: Mainstream sensors provide rapid, breath-by-breath measurements with sharp real-time waveforms. Their optical interfaces can be affected by condensation, secretions, or blood.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 197–198 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Which describe sidestream sampling? Select 3.
options: Analyzer sits directly in the airway
Passes through a filter or water trap to the analyzer
Gas is continuously aspirated near the Y-piece
questions.explanation: Sidestream analyzers aspirate gas continuously from near the airway, pass it through a filter or water trap, and measure it remotely. The textbook describes sidestream sampling as more common and explains transport delay and distortion at high respiratory rates.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 195, 198 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: A neonate breathing at 50/min shows a low, rounded capnogram on sidestream sampling. What is the likely reason?
options: Excess dead space added by the water trap
The analyzer is reading inspired gas only
Mainstream interference from secretions in the airway
High RR (respiratory rate) exceeds the analyzer's response, lowering accuracy
questions.explanation: At high respiratory rates, successive gas samples can mix within a long sidestream catheter, damping waveform peaks and troughs. In small patients, sampling flow can also contaminate exhaled samples with fresh gas.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 198 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Where is a sidestream sampling adapter usually placed?
options: At the Y-piece between the circuit and the airway
In the expiratory limb next to the absorber canister
questions.explanation: The sidestream adapter samples near the airway, typically between the patient and the Y-piece of a circle circuit. The sample travels through tubing and a water trap or filter to a remote analyzer.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 198 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Which law states that the total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures?
questions.explanation: Dalton's law states that the total pressure of a gas mixture is the sum of its component partial pressures. This differs from Henry's law, which concerns gas dissolution in liquids.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 199 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: At 760 mmHg, a gas making up 2% of a dry mixture exerts what partial pressure?
questions.explanation: For a dry gas mixture, partial pressure equals the gas fraction multiplied by total pressure. Two percent of 760 mm Hg is 0.02 × 760 = 15.2 mm Hg, approximately 15 mm Hg.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 199 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: At sea level, what is the partial pressure of 6% CO2 in dry gas?
questions.explanation: For a dry gas mixture at 760 mm Hg, 6% CO2 has partial pressure 0.06 × 760 = 45.6 mm Hg. The closest answer is 46 mm Hg; water-vapor correction is not applied to this explicitly dry mixture.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 199 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Mass spectrometry can identify up to how many gases?
questions.explanation: Mass spec separates ions into a spectrum, identifying up to 8 gases.
questions.citation: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 12

questions.stem: Infrared gas analysis works by measuring what?
options: Energy absorption as light passes through the sample
Ion separation in a magnetic field
Electrical current from a chemical reaction with lead
questions.explanation: Infrared gas analyzers measure absorption of selected infrared wavelengths by molecules such as CO2 and volatile anesthetics. The absorbed energy is used to determine the gas concentration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 200 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Which technique measures the components of a gas mixture by scattered light?
questions.explanation: Raman spectroscopy analyzes wavelength shifts in light scattered by gas molecules. These shifts identify gas constituents rather than measuring infrared absorption.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 204 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Which gases display Raman properties and can be measured by Raman scattering? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Sevoflurane, CO2, and N2O are Raman-active molecules with internal bonds. Monatomic noble gases such as argon, neon, and helium lack the molecular vibrations used for Raman gas analysis.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 204 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Capnometry provides what?
options: A numeric EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) value
questions.explanation: Capnometry refers to the numerical measurement of CO2, commonly end-tidal CO2. Capnography adds a waveform that shows how CO2 varies throughout the respiratory cycle.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 10, printed pp. 241 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Capnometers report results at what conditions?
questions.explanation: Results are reported at body temperature; water vapor can affect accuracy.
questions.citation: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 14

questions.stem: A colorimetric CO2 detector changes from purple to yellow when?
options: After about 10 minutes of continuous use
Only when CO2 is absent from the sample
During inspiration, as fresh gas arrives
During expiration, when CO2 is present
questions.explanation: Exhaled CO2 acidifies the indicator solution, changing metacresol purple from purple to yellow. Inspired CO2-free gas reverses the reaction and returns the indicator toward purple.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 205 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: After intubation, a colorimetric detector stays purple through six breaths. What does this suggest?
options: Right mainstem intubation with one-lung ventilation
No CO2; suspect esophageal tube or no lung perfusion
Correct tracheal placement with good perfusion
A normal detector reading in a ventilated patient
questions.explanation: A persistently purple detector indicates little or no detected exhaled CO2. Esophageal placement and poor pulmonary perfusion must be considered; the color alone is not a definitive diagnosis.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 205; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248

questions.stem: A colorimetric detector cycles purple-yellow after intubation, but breath sounds are absent on the left. What is still possible?
questions.explanation: Exhaled CO2 confirms that sampled gas contains CO2 but does not establish correct tube depth. Mainstem intubation can still produce CO2 detection while one lung is poorly ventilated.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 205; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 244

questions.stem: Where is a colorimetric CO2 detector placed?
options: In the expiratory limb at the absorber
Between the ETT (endotracheal tube) and the circuit
questions.explanation: A colorimetric CO2 detector is interposed between the tracheal tube and the breathing circuit. It samples respired gas to help assess tracheal intubation when conventional capnography is unavailable.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 205 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: O2 analyzers measure what?
questions.explanation: An oxygen analyzer measures the inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2) in the breathing circuit. It does not directly measure arterial oxygen tension, pulse-oximeter saturation, or tissue oxygen consumption.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 207 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: What is the overall reaction in a galvanic (fuel cell) O2 analyzer?
questions.explanation: In a galvanic oxygen cell, oxygen is reduced at the cathode while the lead anode is oxidized. The overall reaction is O2 + 2Pb → 2PbO, producing an electrical signal related to oxygen tension.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 207 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Paramagnetic O2 analyzers rely on what property of oxygen?
options: Attraction to a magnetic field from two unpaired electrons
A chemical reaction with a lead anode that makes current
High solubility in blood and tissue
High infrared absorption at specific wavelengths
questions.explanation: Oxygen has two unpaired electrons and is attracted to a magnetic field, making it paramagnetic. Paramagnetic analyzers use this property to measure oxygen partial pressure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 207 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: A paramagnetic analyzer uses two nitrogen-filled glass spheres. Why nitrogen?
options: Nitrogen absorbs infrared light at the sensor
Nitrogen reacts with lead to make a current
Nitrogen carries the paramagnetic charge itself
N2 isn’t attracted, so O2 in the field displaces them
questions.explanation: A suspended pair of nitrogen-filled spheres is displaced when surrounding paramagnetic oxygen is drawn into the magnetic field. The resulting torque is related to oxygen partial pressure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 207–208 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: What do both fuel cell and paramagnetic analyzers verify?
options: Correct ETT (endotracheal tube) placement in the trachea
The patient is receiving a non-hypoxic mixture
Adequate ventilation and CO2 removal per breath
questions.explanation: Note: both verify the patient is receiving a non-hypoxic mixture.
questions.citation: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slides 16, 17

questions.stem: What waveform is a mirror image of the capnogram?
questions.explanation: The oxygram plots oxygen concentration against time and generally varies opposite to the capnogram. The textbook depicts it as approximately a mirror image, not an exact mathematical inversion.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 208–210 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Nitrogen monitoring can help detect which problems? Select 2.
questions.explanation: Unexpected nitrogen in a breathing system can indicate room-air entrainment from a leak. Nitrogen monitoring can also help detect venous air embolism.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp. 213 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Nitrogen monitoring can be used to judge the adequacy of what?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen monitoring can track washout during preoxygenation. Falling nitrogen indicates replacement of alveolar nitrogen by the supplied oxygen mixture.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 213

questions.stem: How do MAC (minimum alveolar concentration) values of a volatile and N2O combine?
questions.explanation: The textbook describes MAC contributions of nitrous oxide and volatile agents as additive. The displayed sum still depends on the applicable MAC values and patient context.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 213

questions.stem: Running high-flow O2 after turning off the vaporizer has what effect on circuit agent concentration?
questions.explanation: High fresh-gas flow replaces agent-containing circuit gas with fresh gas more rapidly. This accelerates circuit washout after the vaporizer is turned off.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 213

questions.stem: Why does the instructor favor trends over single values for ventilation parameters?
options: Trends are required by accreditation rules
Single values can’t be displayed in real time
Single values are always inaccurate on monitors
Trends reveal bronchospasm, leaks, or kinks early
questions.explanation: Changes in pressure, flow, and volume patterns can reveal developing obstruction or leaks. Comparing trends with the prior pattern can help detect changes that a single isolated value may obscure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed pp. 230–232

questions.stem: Smooth, orderly gas flow is called:
questions.explanation: Laminar flow is smooth and orderly. Turbulent flow contains irregular eddies and vortices.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 224

questions.stem: Which factors convert laminar flow to turbulent? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Higher flow and disturbances such as kinks or narrowed passages can promote turbulence. The transition depends on gas properties and the geometry of the flow path.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed pp. 224–225

questions.stem: Which gas property increases the tendency toward turbulent flow?
questions.explanation: Higher gas density promotes turbulence at comparable flow and geometry. Density is one of the properties governing the transition from orderly to chaotic flow.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed pp. 224–225

questions.stem: A crack in a rotameter's glass tube causes what?
options: A higher float reading with correct delivery
A leak that changes the amount delivered
questions.explanation: A cracked flow tube can leak gas and alter the amount reaching the patient. The displayed float position therefore does not guarantee intact downstream delivery.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 225

questions.stem: Rotameters are which type of device?
options: Graduated glass tubes measuring gas, vapor, or liquid flow
Fuel cells measuring the O2 fraction
questions.explanation: A rotameter uses a float in a tapered, calibrated tube to indicate flow. The calibration depends on the tube, float, fluid, and operating conditions.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 225

questions.stem: A pneumotachometer measures flow from what?
options: Pressure drop as gas passes a known resistance
Rotation of a vane in the gas stream
Absorption of infrared light by the gas
Heat lost from a heated wire in the flow
questions.explanation: A pneumotachometer measures the pressure difference across a known resistance. That pressure difference is converted to flow using the characteristics of the device.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 226

questions.stem: Spirometry is the most common test of which part of respiratory function?
questions.explanation: Spirometry assesses ventilatory volumes and flows. It does not directly measure pulmonary perfusion, diffusion capacity, or blood oxygen transport.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 230

questions.stem: FEV1 is:
options: Volume forcibly exhaled in the first second
Peak flow reached during forced inspiration
Volume left in the lungs after full exhalation
Total volume exhaled after a full inhalation
questions.explanation: FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) is the volume forcibly exhaled during the first second of a forced expiration. It differs from total forced vital capacity and from a peak flow rate.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 230

questions.stem: On a volume-time curve, inspiration appears as what?
questions.explanation: Inspiration increases the plotted lung volume, producing an upslope. Exhalation produces the downslope in the conventional volume-time display.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 230

questions.stem: Volume-time curves help identify which problems? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Volume-time curves can reveal incomplete return toward baseline or an abnormal excursion below it. The cited examples include air trapping, expiratory leaks, and flow-transducer miscalibration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed pp. 230–231

questions.stem: On these volume-time curves, which panel suggests an expiratory leak or air trapping?
questions.explanation: Panel B does not return to the starting volume baseline. The cited pattern can occur with an expiratory leak or retained gas and must be interpreted with the rest of the monitoring data.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 231

questions.stem: On these volume-time curves, which panel suggests forced exhalation or a miscalibrated flow transducer?
questions.explanation: Panel C extends below the volume baseline. The textbook associates this pattern with active exhalation or inaccurate flow-transducer calibration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 231

questions.stem: Which panel shows a normal volume-time curve?
questions.explanation: Panel A rises during inspiration and returns to baseline during exhalation. It matches the normal volume-time pattern in the cited figure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 231

questions.stem: Which flow-time panel matches volume-controlled ventilation with constant inspiratory flow?
questions.explanation: Panel A has a square inspiratory flow waveform, meaning constant inspiratory flow. That is the classic volume-control pattern.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed pp. 230–231

questions.stem: Which flow-time panel shows a decelerating inspiratory flow pattern?
questions.explanation: Panel B's inspiratory flow peaks early and decays, typical of pressure control.
questions.citation: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slides 30, 32

questions.stem: In panel C, expiratory flow has not returned to zero when the next breath starts. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: Expiratory flow persisting when the next inspiration begins indicates incomplete expiration. This supports air trapping and possible intrinsic PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) rather than normal completion of passive exhalation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 231

questions.stem: Loop A is a normal mechanical breath. Loop D is the same breath after PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) is applied. How does PEEP change the pressure-volume loop?
options: It makes the loop show both positive and negative pressures
It shifts the loop to negative pressures
It shifts the loop so it shows only positive pressure
It has no effect on the loop
questions.explanation: Compare where each loop starts. Loop A begins at zero pressure, while loop D begins to the right at the PEEP level, so the whole breath stays in positive pressure. The shape is similar because compliance has not changed; only the baseline moved.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 231

questions.stem: Loop C is from a spontaneously breathing patient with no PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure). What does the loop show?
options: Only positive pressures above PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure)
questions.explanation: In loop C, inspiration (blue) swings left of the zero line as the diaphragm creates negative pressure, and expiration (red) swings right into positive pressure. Mechanical breaths without patient effort stay on the positive side.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 231

questions.stem: Which problems can an abnormal pressure-volume loop reveal? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Pressure-volume loops can change with respiratory compliance, tube position, or equipment problems. The cited examples include endobronchial intubation and altered mechanics after a malfunction.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 232

questions.stem: The instructor calls which monitor the most valuable?
questions.explanation: A capnograph displays a CO2 waveform as well as numerical values. That waveform helps assess ventilation and may also reveal changes in metabolism or circulation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 239

questions.stem: On this capnogram, which numbered point marks where EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) is measured?
questions.explanation: Point 5 is at the end of expiration, just before the inspiratory downstroke. This is the usual location of the end-tidal CO2 measurement.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 239–240

questions.stem: Which numbered segment is the alveolar plateau (phase III)?
questions.explanation: Segment 3 is the alveolar plateau, phase III. Its shape reflects the progressive emptying of alveolar gas during expiration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 240

questions.stem: Segment 4 on this capnogram represents what?
questions.explanation: Segment 4 is the inspiratory downstroke, phase 0. Inspired low-CO2 gas rapidly replaces expired gas at the sampling site.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 240

questions.stem: Segment 1 should read what value in a normal capnogram?
questions.explanation: Segment 1 is the low-CO2 baseline, normally close to 0 mmHg. A persistently elevated baseline raises concern for inspired CO2 or another sampling or circuit problem.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 240–242

questions.stem: Segment 2 becomes much less steep. What is the most likely cause?
options: Return of spontaneous breathing as paralysis fades
Expiratory airflow obstruction such as bronchospasm
questions.explanation: A less steep expiratory upstroke can indicate obstructed exhalation, as with bronchospasm or a kinked tube. The waveform should prompt assessment rather than being treated as a unique diagnosis.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 242

questions.stem: Which capnogram panel is consistent with bronchospasm?
questions.explanation: Panel A has the sloping, shark-fin appearance associated with expiratory obstruction. Bronchospasm is one possible cause; tube obstruction can create a similar pattern.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 242

questions.stem: Which capnogram panel shows rebreathing?
questions.explanation: Panel C has an elevated inspiratory baseline, consistent with inspired CO2 and rebreathing. Valve incompetence or exhausted absorbent are possible causes in a circle system.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 242

questions.stem: Which capnogram panel shows a curare cleft?
questions.explanation: Panel D shows an interruption of the alveolar plateau associated with spontaneous respiratory effort during controlled ventilation. The cited text calls this a curare cleft.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18, printed p. 318; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 243

questions.stem: A patient's waveform looks like panel D. What is the best interpretation?
options: There is a large cuff leak around the ETT (endotracheal tube)
Paralysis is wearing off and the patient is breathing
The CO2 absorbent is exhausted and needs changing
questions.explanation: The cleft reflects spontaneous effort during a mechanical breath.
questions.citation: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.stem: A waveform changes from panel B to panel C over 30 minutes. FIRST check?
options: ETT (endotracheal tube) position, looking for esophageal intubation
CO2 absorbent and unidirectional valve function
questions.explanation: The elevated inspiratory baseline in panel C suggests rebreathing. Checking the absorbent and unidirectional valves is appropriate among these choices.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 242

questions.stem: Which capnography trend panel fits cardiac arrest?
questions.explanation: A sudden drop toward zero with continued ventilation suggests loss of pulmonary blood flow.
questions.citation: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.stem: Which trend panel fits return of spontaneous circulation during CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation)?
questions.explanation: A sudden rise from low values signals restored pulmonary blood flow (ROSC).
questions.citation: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.stem: Which trend panel fits hypoventilation?
questions.explanation: Gradually rising EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) with each breath fits hypoventilation (or rising CO2 production).
questions.citation: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.stem: Which trend panel fits hyperventilation?
questions.explanation: Gradually falling EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) fits hyperventilation (or falling CO2 production).
questions.citation: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.stem: EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) drops abruptly to near zero as in panel C while airway pressures are unchanged and the circuit is intact. What should you suspect first?
options: Hyperventilation from an increase in rate
Loss of cardiac output or massive embolism
questions.explanation: A sudden CO2 loss with an apparently intact airway and circuit raises concern for sharply reduced pulmonary perfusion. Loss of cardiac output or a major embolic event is a possibility, not a diagnosis established by the waveform alone.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18, printed p. 318

questions.stem: Why do providers hyperventilate patients with raised ICP (intracranial pressure)?
options: Lower CO2 causes cerebral vasoconstriction, lowering blood flow
Lower CO2 causes cerebral vasodilation, raising blood flow
Hyperventilation raises CO2 to protect neurons
questions.explanation: Lower PaCO2 (arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide) causes cerebral vasoconstriction and reduces cerebral blood flow, which can reduce intracranial blood volume. Excessive hypocapnia can also compromise cerebral oxygen delivery, so this is a physiologic explanation rather than a universal treatment target.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 247

questions.stem: Why does the lecture stress EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) monitoring during transport of a patient with raised ICP?
options: Transport monitors can’t display SpO2 (peripheral oxygen saturation) reliably
EtCO2 replaces the need for an arterial line
CO2 swings change cerebral blood flow and ICP
questions.explanation: Changes in PaCO2 (arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide) can alter cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure. Capnography helps detect ventilation changes during transport, but it does not directly measure ICP or replace assessment of arterial CO2 when needed.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 247–248

questions.stem: Under normal conditions, CO2 is excreted how?
options: As fast as it is made, with no net change
Slower than it is made, so body stores rise
In bursts during the expiratory pause
Faster than it is made, so body stores fall
questions.explanation: In a steady state, pulmonary CO2 elimination matches total body production. If ventilation changes abruptly, body stores can temporarily make elimination differ from production.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 245

questions.stem: Which change would raise CO2 production?
options: Increased metabolism, such as fever or MH (malignant hyperthermia)
questions.explanation: Increased metabolic activity, including fever or malignant hyperthermia, can increase CO2 delivery and production. The resulting end-tidal value also depends on ventilation and perfusion.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18, printed p. 318

questions.stem: EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) varies breath to breath based on which factors? Select 3.
questions.explanation: The amount of CO2 eliminated in each breath depends on tidal volume, dead space, and effective alveolar ventilation. These interacting factors make single-breath measurements variable.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 245

questions.stem: What does a circuit leak do to EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) accuracy?
options: Raises it falsely to arterial levels
questions.explanation: Room air entering a leaking sampling line can dilute the sampled CO2. The displayed end-tidal value may then fail to reflect the patient’s true expired concentration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 245

questions.stem: Dead space is best described as:
questions.explanation: Alveolar dead space is ventilation reaching alveoli that receive little or no effective perfusion. That ventilation contributes little to gas exchange.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 245–246

questions.stem: Physiologic dead space equals:
options: Alveolar dead space minus anatomic dead space
Tidal volume minus alveolar volume only at rest
Airway (anatomic) dead space plus alveolar dead space
questions.explanation: Patient physiologic dead space combines conducting-airway and alveolar dead space. External apparatus can add further ineffective ventilation and should be considered separately in this wording.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 245–246
