questions.stem: How does a large increase in alveolar dead space change the PaCO2-EtCO2 gradient?
options: Has no effect, since both values fall together
Reverses it, so EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) exceeds PaCO2 (arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide)
Widens it, because EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) falls while PaCO2 (arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide) does not
Narrows it, because EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) rises toward PaCO2 (arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide)
questions.explanation: In the illustrated dead-space model, low-CO2 gas from underperfused alveoli dilutes expired gas. End-tidal CO2 falls relative to arterial CO2, widening the gradient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 243–244

questions.stem: Which conditions increase dead space (V/Q mismatch) and lower EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide)? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Pulmonary embolism, hypovolemia, and alveolar overdistension can reduce perfusion relative to ventilation. The resulting alveolar dead space can lower end-tidal CO2 relative to arterial CO2.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 246

questions.stem: Per the instructor, capnography changes from dead space often appear when?
options: After SpO2 (peripheral oxygen saturation) has started to fall
questions.explanation: Note: EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) often changes before hemodynamic changes appear.
questions.citation: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 40

questions.stem: During CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation), what PETCO2 (partial pressure of end-tidal carbon dioxide) indicates sufficient pulmonary blood flow from compressions?
questions.explanation: The cited discussion uses a value greater than approximately 10 mmHg during stable minute ventilation as evidence of potentially survivable pulmonary blood flow. It does not guarantee adequate CPR or determine prognosis by itself.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248

questions.stem: During CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation), PETCO2 (partial pressure of end-tidal carbon dioxide) is 6 mmHg. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: Low end-tidal CO2 during CPR should prompt assessment of compression quality and other reversible causes of low pulmonary flow. It is not, by itself, a reason to stop resuscitation or automatically increase ventilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248

questions.stem: Why is pulmonary embolism hard to diagnose with capnography alone?
options: Capnography can’t reflect dead space changes
PE characteristically raises EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide)
PE has no effect on CO2 elimination
Baseline alveolar dead space is usually unknown
questions.explanation: The baseline alveolar dead space is often unknown, and several other conditions can reduce pulmonary perfusion. A low end-tidal value therefore cannot uniquely diagnose pulmonary embolism.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 249

questions.stem: During sedation cases, capnography helps detect what?
questions.explanation: Capnography can detect respiratory obstruction and inadequate ventilation during sedation. Supplemental oxygen can delay a fall in SpO2 (peripheral oxygen saturation) even while ventilation deteriorates.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 249

questions.stem: Functional saturation (SaO2) is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Functional saturation is O2Hb (oxyhemoglobin) divided by O2Hb plus reduced hemoglobin. Dyshemoglobins are excluded from that denominator.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 253

questions.stem: Why does fractional saturation read lower than functional saturation with significant carbon monoxide?
options: Functional saturation counts COHb (carboxyhemoglobin) as oxygenated
The two values are identical in CO poisoning
Fractional includes COHb (carboxyhemoglobin) and MetHb (methemoglobin) in the denominator
questions.explanation: Fractional saturation includes COHb and MetHb in the denominator. With substantial COHb, it can therefore be lower than functional saturation for the same oxyhemoglobin concentration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 253

questions.stem: In CaO2 (arterial oxygen content) = 1.34 × Hb × SaO2 (arterial oxygen saturation) + 0.003 × PaO2 (arterial partial pressure of oxygen), what does 0.003 × PaO2 represent?
questions.explanation: The 0.003 × PaO2 term represents oxygen dissolved in plasma. The much larger hemoglobin-bound component is represented by the first term.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 253

questions.stem: Hb (hemoglobin) 10 g/dL, SaO2 (arterial oxygen saturation) 100%, PaO2 (arterial partial pressure of oxygen) 100 mmHg. What is CaO2 (arterial oxygen content)?
questions.explanation: Convert 100% saturation to a fraction of 1.0. CaO2 = 1.34 × 10 × 1.0 + 0.003 × 100 = 13.7 mL/dL.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 253

questions.stem: Oxygen delivery to tissues depends on CaO2 (arterial oxygen content) and what?
questions.explanation: Oxygen delivery depends on arterial oxygen content and cardiac output. A normal saturation therefore does not guarantee adequate tissue delivery when hemoglobin or cardiac output is low.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 254

questions.stem: How many O2 binding sites does each hemoglobin molecule have?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin has four oxygen-binding subunits. Binding of oxygen to one subunit facilitates binding at the others, contributing to the sigmoidal dissociation curve.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 628

questions.stem: The Beer-Lambert law is written as:
questions.explanation: Absorbance is proportional to absorber concentration and optical path length: A = εcl. The proportionality coefficient depends on the absorber and wavelength.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed pp. 255–256

questions.stem: In the Beer-Lambert law, what does "l" stand for?
questions.explanation: The symbol l denotes the optical path length through the absorbing material. Increasing that path length increases absorbance when the other variables are unchanged.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed pp. 255–256

questions.stem: Per Beer-Lambert, doubling the concentration of an absorber while holding path length constant does what to absorbance?
questions.explanation: At a fixed wavelength and path length, absorbance is proportional to concentration. Doubling the concentration therefore doubles absorbance under the law’s assumptions.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed pp. 255–256

questions.stem: Which device relies on the Beer-Lambert law?
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry uses wavelength-dependent light absorption to estimate hemoglobin saturation. Its clinical algorithms require additional calibration because living tissue is more complex than a transparent laboratory solution.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed pp. 255–256

questions.stem: Fetal hemoglobin has what effect on pulse oximetry?
questions.explanation: HbF: no effect (note: HgF okay).
questions.citation: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 50

questions.stem: Which can cause pulse oximetry errors? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Methemoglobin and intravenous dyes can alter optical absorption, while nail coatings can interfere with light transmission. The magnitude depends on the substance, sensor, and device; nail-polish effects are variable.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 258

questions.stem: Why do dyshemoglobins such as methemoglobin cause pulse oximetry errors?
options: They increase perfusion at the probe site
They can’t carry O2 but still absorb light
They carry O2 more efficiently than normal Hb
They are invisible to the oximeter’s light
questions.explanation: Dyshemoglobins can absorb the oximeter’s light without carrying oxygen normally. A conventional two-wavelength algorithm can misinterpret that absorption as ordinary oxyhemoglobin or reduced hemoglobin.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed pp. 257–258

questions.stem: Per the instructor, which finger has the most perfusion for probe placement?
questions.explanation: Note: middle finger has the most perfusion.
questions.citation: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 50

questions.stem: How do modern oximeters reduce motion artifact?
options: Longer signal averaging and ECG (electrocardiogram) synchronization
Using a single wavelength of light
Increasing the light intensity at the probe site
questions.explanation: Earlier devices used longer averaging and ECG synchronization to reduce motion-related errors. Averaging slows response, and the cited ECG synchronization feature was abandoned in later models.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 260

questions.stem: SpO2 (peripheral oxygen saturation) is determined from which signal?
questions.explanation: The described adaptive-filtering approach estimates the motion-related noise and subtracts it from the total signal. Saturation is then calculated from the remaining signal; this is not a universal description of every oximeter algorithm.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 260

questions.stem: A dependent probe position can lower SpO2 (peripheral oxygen saturation) by up to how much?
questions.explanation: The cited volunteer study found decreases as large as 8% when the arm moved from raised to dependent. Venous pulsations can contaminate the signal, so this is a study finding rather than a fixed change with every dependent probe.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 260

questions.stem: A patient on 100% O2 has PaO2 (arterial partial pressure of oxygen) falling from 450 to 150 mmHg, but SpO2 (peripheral oxygen saturation) stays 100%. What limitation does this show?
options: SpO2 gives no early warning of falling PaO2
The probe is malpositioned on the finger
Pulse oximetry overestimates PaO2 at all levels
questions.explanation: At high PaO2, the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve is nearly flat. A substantial fall in oxygen tension can therefore occur while SpO2 remains close to 100%.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 266

questions.stem: Pulse oximetry became standard of care in what year?
questions.explanation: The textbook identifies 1986 as the year pulse oximetry became a standard of care in the operating room. This is the historical adoption milestone described in the source.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed pp. 255, 265

questions.stem: Where is hypoxemia more common?
options: Neither; hypoxemia is rare after surgery
questions.explanation: The cited discussion reports greater hypoxemia risk in the PACU than in the operating room for many patients. Residual anesthetic effects persist after the protected airway and controlled ventilation have ended.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 265

questions.stem: Which patient factors are associated with postoperative desaturation? Select 3.
questions.explanation: The reported postoperative desaturation associations include obesity, advanced age, and extensive surgery. These are population-level risk associations rather than a guarantee of desaturation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 265

questions.stem: Which situation is a classic setup for postoperative desaturation?
options: Supine position with O2 by mask
Arrival in PACU (postanesthesia care unit) on a nonrebreather
Transport to PACU (postanesthesia care unit) without supplemental O2
questions.explanation: The cited transport studies found frequent desaturation when supplemental oxygen was not provided. Transport monitoring and oxygen needs must be planned for the patient’s condition.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 265

questions.stem: Peak pressure rises suddenly with a shark-fin capnogram. Which cause fits both?
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm increases airway resistance and can produce a sloping expiratory capnogram. The resistive load can also increase peak airway pressure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 242; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152

questions.stem: Airway pressure and EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) both fall to near zero suddenly. Most likely cause?
questions.explanation: A sudden loss of both circuit pressure and exhaled CO2 is consistent with a circuit disconnection. The airway, circuit, sampling system, and patient still require immediate assessment.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 241–242

questions.stem: Infrared analyzers are categorized as which two types?
questions.explanation: Dispersive analyzers separate the spectrum into component wavelengths. Nondispersive analyzers use selected wavelength bands to detect the gases of interest.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 200

questions.stem: The process of eliminating CO2 is called:
questions.explanation: Ventilation moves fresh gas into the lungs and removes CO2-containing gas on exhalation. Oxygenation concerns transfer of oxygen into arterial blood and can change independently.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 151

questions.stem: Gas solubility in a liquid is directly proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid. This is:
questions.explanation: Henry’s law relates the amount dissolved in a liquid to the gas’s partial pressure above it. The relationship also depends on solubility and the specified temperature.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 19, printed p. 434

questions.stem: How does systemic vascular tone respond to low O2 or high CO2?
questions.explanation: The normal cerebral vascular response to hypercarbia is vasodilation. Hypocapnia produces vasoconstriction, so the vascular bed and CO2 direction must be specified.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 91

questions.stem: Filling the lungs with O2 so tissues are supplied without ventilation is called:
questions.explanation: Apneic oxygenation supplies oxygen without normal tidal ventilation when the airway and oxygen pathway remain open. It does not provide adequate CO2 elimination or guarantee unlimited safe apnea.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 151

questions.stem: During spontaneous inspiration, diaphragm contraction makes intrathoracic pressure:
questions.explanation: Diaphragm contraction lowers intrathoracic pressure during spontaneous inspiration. The resulting pressure gradient draws gas into the lungs.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 620

questions.stem: Change in lung volume per change in pressure is called:
questions.explanation: Compliance is the change in volume per unit change in pressure. Lower compliance means more pressure is needed for the same volume change.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152

questions.stem: Pulmonary fibrosis has what effect on compliance?
options: Increases it only at high volumes
questions.explanation: Fibrosis makes the lungs harder to inflate and decreases compliance. A given volume change therefore requires a larger distending pressure.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 620

questions.stem: Bronchoconstriction or ETT (endotracheal tube) obstruction has what effect on resistance?
questions.explanation: Bronchoconstriction or tube obstruction increases resistance to flow. At a comparable inspiratory flow, this increases the resistive pressure requirement.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 232

questions.stem: Volume equals:
questions.explanation: At constant flow, delivered volume equals flow multiplied by delivery time. With variable flow, volume is the integral of flow over time.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 153

questions.stem: Flow multiplied by resistance gives:
questions.explanation: Flow multiplied by resistance gives the resistive pressure drop. Total airway pressure can also include elastic pressure and PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure).
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152

questions.stem: Airway pressure equals:
questions.explanation: In the passive model, airway pressure includes resistive pressure, elastic pressure, and baseline PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure). Those components are flow × resistance, volume/compliance, and PEEP.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 620

questions.stem: Alveolar pressure equals:
questions.explanation: At a no-flow hold, the resistive pressure drop disappears. Plateau pressure is then approximated by tidal volume/compliance plus PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) in the passive linear model.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 620

questions.stem: A patient develops bronchospasm during volume control. Which term of the airway pressure equation rises?
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm increases resistance. With the same set volume and inspiratory flow, the flow × resistance pressure component rises.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152

questions.stem: Pneumoperitoneum is established during volume control. Which term of the airway pressure equation rises most?
questions.explanation: Pneumoperitoneum can increase the elastic load on the respiratory system. At the same delivered volume, lower compliance raises the volume/compliance pressure component.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Which are among the four main components of a mechanical ventilator? Select 3.
questions.explanation: A ventilator needs a power source and controls to deliver the selected breathing pattern. Safety features and alarms help detect unsafe pressure, volume, or ventilation conditions.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–163; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: A piston ventilator's drive force comes from:
questions.explanation: An electric motor drives the piston. This separates the driving force from compressed gas used for a conventional bellows system.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 161

questions.stem: A bellows ventilator's drive force comes from:
options: An electric motor moving a piston
Compressed driving gas squeezing the bellows
questions.explanation: Compressed driving gas outside the bellows compresses the patient-gas compartment. The drive gas is normally separate from the gas delivered to the patient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–161

questions.stem: Ascending bellows rise during which phase?
questions.explanation: Ascending bellows rise as they refill during expiration. Their compression delivers gas during inspiration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 160

questions.stem: What happens to ascending bellows with a circuit disconnection?
options: They rise normally from room air entrainment
They fail to rise fully or collapse
They lock in the inspiratory position
questions.explanation: A significant disconnection can prevent proper refilling of ascending bellows. Bellows movement is a useful clue but does not replace pressure, volume, and CO2 monitoring.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 160

questions.stem: What happens to descending bellows with a circuit disconnection?
options: They rise to the top of the housing
They stop moving and lock in place
They still fill with room air and look normal
They collapse immediately and stay down
questions.explanation: A weighted descending bellows can draw in room air and continue to move despite a disconnect. Apparently normal bellows movement therefore does not prove effective patient ventilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 160

questions.stem: Why are ascending bellows considered safer for detecting disconnection?
options: They have a higher relief valve opening pressure
They entrain room air during a disconnect
They use an electric motor as the drive
Ascending bellows need exhaled gas to rise
questions.explanation: A disconnected circuit means the bellows don't refill, an obvious visual sign.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 16, 17

questions.stem: The ascending bellows spill (relief) valve opens at about what pressure?
questions.explanation: The ascending bellows spill valve opens at about 2–4 cmH2O (lecture), which adds a little baseline PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure). Nurse Anesthesia describes about 2–3 cmH2O for this design.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 16; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed pp. 275–276

questions.stem: What side effect does the ascending bellows spill valve produce?
options: A small amount of baseline PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure)
questions.explanation: The weighted relief-valve mechanism can leave a small positive pressure at end expiration. This is the baseline PEEP described for the standing-bellows design.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 275

questions.stem: Which safety features help detect disconnection with descending bellows on newer machines? Select 3.
options: Sensors detecting failure to return to full hang
A spill valve opening at 75 cmH2O
questions.explanation: Because descending bellows can look normal, alarms and sensors are needed.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 17

questions.stem: Which are consequences of a hole in the bellows? Select 3.
options: Altered FiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen) depending on drive gas
Lower airway pressure at the patient
questions.explanation: A bellows perforation can allow driving gas to enter the patient circuit. This can alter oxygen concentration, dilute the volatile agent, and expose the patient to excessive pressure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–161

questions.stem: A bellows leak develops on a machine using 100% O2 as drive gas. How does FiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen) change?
options: It falls only if N2O is in use
questions.explanation: If oxygen driving gas enters a patient mixture with a lower oxygen fraction, FiO2 can rise toward 100%. The amount depends on leak size and the circuit conditions.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–161

questions.stem: A bellows leak develops on a machine using an air/O2 drive gas while delivering 100% O2. How does FiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen) change?
questions.explanation: Mixing an air-containing driving gas into a 100%-oxygen patient circuit lowers the oxygen fraction. The volatile-agent concentration can also be diluted.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 161

questions.stem: Expired agent drops unexpectedly with ascending bellows and normal vaporizer function. Which equipment problem fits?
options: Bellows leak releasing agent on expiration
questions.explanation: In ascending bellows, a leak lets agent escape on expiration, diluting the anesthetic.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 18

questions.stem: Which ventilator does NOT need driving gas?
options: Pneumatic bellows with an air drive
questions.explanation: The piston is driven by an electric motor. It therefore does not require a compressed-gas driving circuit like the listed bellows systems.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 161

questions.stem: During an O2 pipeline failure with only a cylinder available, which ventilator type conserves O2 best?
options: Any bellows ventilator with high FGF (fresh gas flow)
Piston, since it needs no driving gas
questions.explanation: A piston ventilator does not consume oxygen as driving gas. During pipeline failure, this can conserve the remaining cylinder supply for the patient.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 276

questions.stem: A piston ventilator's positive pressure relief valve opens at:
questions.explanation: The described Apollo piston pressure-relief valve opens at about 75 ±5 cmH2O. This value belongs to that device description rather than every piston ventilator.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 276

questions.stem: A piston ventilator's negative pressure relief valve opens at:
questions.explanation: In the described Apollo system, the negative-pressure relief valve opens at −8 cmH2O. It admits room air to protect against excessive negative pressure.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 276

questions.stem: A piston's negative pressure relief valve opens repeatedly during a case with low FGF (fresh gas flow). What is the main risk?
options: Room air entrainment dilutes agent, risking awareness
Rising agent concentration in the circuit
questions.explanation: Room-air entrainment can dilute both oxygen and volatile anesthetic in the circuit. Agent dilution can increase awareness risk even though the valve protects against negative pressure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 174

questions.stem: Negative end-expiratory pressure (NEEP) is a recognized risk of which ventilator?
options: Turbine in CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) mode
questions.explanation: Piston retraction can generate negative pressure if gas supply or reservoir volume is inadequate. Protective relief valves limit that risk but can introduce room air.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 276

questions.stem: Fresh gas decoupling is a feature of which ventilator type?
questions.explanation: The described Apollo and Fabius systems use piston-driven ventilation with fresh-gas decoupling. Decoupling is a circuit feature and should not be assumed from a drive label alone.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 276, 280

questions.stem: During inspiration with fresh gas decoupling, where does fresh gas go?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, the decoupling valve prevents fresh gas from augmenting the delivered tidal volume. Fresh gas is diverted into the manual reservoir bag.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 280

questions.stem: During expiration with fresh gas decoupling, where does fresh gas go?
options: Out to the scavenger through the APL (adjustable pressure-limiting valve)
Into the reservoir bag, bypassing the piston
Into the piston to fill it for the next breath
questions.explanation: During expiration, the decoupling valve opens and the piston refills. The refill includes exhaled gas and fresh gas stored in the reservoir bag.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed pp. 280–281

questions.stem: With fresh gas decoupling, raising FGF (fresh gas flow) from 2 to 8 L/min changes delivered tidal volume how?
options: It increases with the extra flow
It decreases as gas is vented
questions.explanation: Properly functioning fresh-gas decoupling separates inspiratory tidal volume from fresh-gas flow changes. Raising fresh-gas flow alone therefore does not augment the set delivered volume.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 280

questions.stem: Without fresh gas decoupling, raising FGF (fresh gas flow) during volume control has what effect on delivered tidal volume?
options: It has no effect on delivered volume
It decreases only at high respiratory rates
It increases, because fresh gas adds to each breath
It decreases, because the extra fresh gas is vented
questions.explanation: Fresh gas entering during inspiration can add to tidal volume in an uncompensated system. Decoupling or electronic fresh-gas compensation prevents this source of augmentation.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 280

questions.stem: Which are benefits of fresh gas decoupling? Select 2.
options: Higher delivered Vt at high FGF (fresh gas flow)
questions.explanation: Decoupling helps maintain set tidal volume when fresh-gas flow changes. This supports stable ventilation while flow is adjusted for a low-flow technique.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 280

questions.stem: In a decoupled piston circuit, the reservoir bag inflates and deflates with each breath during mechanical ventilation. What does this reflect?
options: The APL (adjustable pressure-limiting) valve is stuck in the closed position
The decoupling valve has failed in the open position
Normal function of a decoupled piston system
A disconnection at the Y-piece is present
questions.explanation: In this circuit, the bag fills with fresh gas during inspiration and empties toward the piston during expiration. Its movement during mechanical ventilation is therefore expected.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 280

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of a piston ventilator?
options: It adapts easily to non-rebreathing circuits
It is loud, so cycling is easy to hear
It adds no PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) to the system
questions.explanation: Advantages: no PEEP, precise Vt (tidal volume), compliance/leak compensation, decoupling, useful in pipeline failure.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 22

questions.stem: Which are disadvantages of piston ventilators? Select 3.
options: Adds a baseline PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) to the system
Requires O2 as its driving gas
Quiet, so cycling may not be heard
Not easily adapted to non-rebreathing circuits
questions.explanation: The cited piston-system disadvantages include potential negative pressure, quiet cycling, and difficulty adapting some designs to nonrebreathing circuits. These limitations are device-dependent rather than universal behavior of every model.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 276

questions.stem: Why do piston ventilators deliver more precise tidal volumes?
options: Compliance/leak compensation and fresh gas decoupling
Absence of a reservoir bag anywhere in the circuit
A spill valve that adds a little PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure)
Higher driving gas pressure in the housing
questions.explanation: Compliance and leak compensation reduce volume losses, while fresh-gas decoupling prevents extra flow from changing tidal volume. The rigid piston structure also reduces compliance-related loss.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 276

questions.stem: A turbine ventilator raises circuit pressure during inspiration by doing what?
options: Opening a solenoid to the pipeline
Moving a piston with a motor
questions.explanation: Increasing turbine speed increases the driving pressure. Sensors and electronic feedback regulate the resulting pressures and flows.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 162, 175

questions.stem: Which are listed benefits of turbine ventilators? Select 2.
options: Built-in negative pressure protection at −8 cmH2O
Added PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) from a spill valve
Use of O2 as drive gas
questions.explanation: Continuous turbine-driven circulation promotes mixing and reduces circuit dead space in the described design. It still requires electricity and appropriate pressure and flow control.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 162

questions.stem: Solenoid valves control gas flow by:
options: A bimetallic strip that bends with heat
A float rising in a tapered tube
Pneumatic pressure from the pipeline only
An electric current creating a magnetic field
questions.explanation: Current through the coil produces a magnetic field that moves the solenoid mechanism. This electrically controlled movement opens or closes the gas pathway.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 162

questions.stem: Which cycling mechanism do most anesthesia ventilators use in controlled modes?
questions.explanation: In the described controlled modes, respiratory rate and I:E timing govern cycling. Pressure, flow, and volume targets can still modify delivery or terminate a breath in particular designs.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 162

questions.stem: In time-cycled ventilation, what ends inspiration?
options: Flow falling to a preset value
questions.explanation: Time-cycled inspiration ends when the preset inspiratory time has elapsed. Respiratory rate and the I:E ratio determine the time available for each phase.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 162

questions.stem: Which is a drawback of time-cycled controlled ventilation?
options: Ventilation stops with low respiratory drive
questions.explanation: A mandatory breath delivered out of step with patient effort can produce dyssynchrony. Synchronized or supported modes can help match delivery to spontaneous breathing.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed pp. 277–278

questions.stem: In flow-cycled ventilation, inspiration ends when:
options: Flow drops to a preset value
questions.explanation: Flow cycling ends inspiration when inspiratory flow falls to the selected threshold. The pressure-support example in Figure 6.22 uses a fraction of peak flow rather than a fixed inspiratory duration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 162; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168

questions.stem: Per the instructor, flow cycling is typically set to end inspiration at about what percent of peak flow?
questions.explanation: Note: set to stop I at about 20%, then switch to E.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 26

questions.stem: How does poor compliance affect tidal volume in flow-cycled modes?
questions.explanation: At an unchanged pressure target and comparable inspiratory timing, reduced compliance can reduce tidal volume. Pressure-targeted delivery therefore requires volume monitoring.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 166

questions.stem: In older volume-cycled ventilators, what varies with compliance and resistance?
questions.explanation: Volume is fixed; pressure and flow vary, with a higher pneumothorax risk.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 27

questions.stem: Older pressure-cycled ventilators have what drawback with poor compliance?
options: Increased pneumothorax risk from fixed volume
questions.explanation: A pressure-cycled ventilator ends inspiration when the selected pressure is reached. With reduced compliance, that pressure can be reached after a smaller volume has entered the lungs, reducing tidal volume.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 152, 162

questions.stem: Per the instructor, what FiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen) is typical during maintenance?
questions.explanation: Note: maintenance 30–50%; high fractions for preox, induction, emergence.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 31

questions.stem: Why use a low FiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen) during maintenance?
options: Reduce airway fire risk and O2 toxicity
questions.explanation: Unnecessary high oxygen concentrations increase exposure in patients susceptible to oxygen toxicity and can increase airway fire risk near an ignition source. Oxygen must still be sufficient for adequate oxygenation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 211

questions.stem: When are high FiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen) values appropriate? Select 2.
options: Routine maintenance of a healthy patient
questions.explanation: High oxygen is described for preoxygenation and during recovery from inhaled anesthesia. Oxygen concentration must still account for airway-fire risk and patient-specific concerns.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 211; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 83

questions.stem: To maintain EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) of about 30–40 mmHg in a typical adult, the lecture suggests what RR (respiratory rate)?
questions.explanation: RR 10–16 for EtCO2 about 30–40.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 32

questions.stem: Per the instructor, EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) typically runs how much below PaCO2 (arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide)?
questions.explanation: End-tidal CO2 is approximately 2–5 mmHg below arterial CO2 in patients without cardiopulmonary abnormalities. Increased dead space or hemodynamic changes can widen this difference, so the approximation is conditional.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18, printed p. 316

questions.stem: Near emergence, why might you lower the ventilator rate?
options: Allow CO2 to rise and stimulate respiratory drive
Lower CO2 to deepen the anesthetic before waking
questions.explanation: If alveolar ventilation decreases, CO2 can rise and increase respiratory drive as anesthetic depression resolves. This is a physiologic explanation, not a universal instruction to reduce ventilation near extubation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 151; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248

questions.stem: When low tidal volume ventilation is used, what often must change to manage CO2?
options: PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) must be removed
FiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen) must increase
questions.explanation: Reducing tidal volume reduces minute ventilation unless respiratory rate increases. A higher rate may therefore be needed to preserve alveolar ventilation and CO2 elimination, with allowance for dead-space ventilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 151–153

questions.stem: Laparoscopic CO2 insufflation tends to do what to EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) at constant ventilation?
questions.explanation: Absorbed insufflation CO2 increases the amount of CO2 the lungs must eliminate. At fixed minute ventilation, pneumoperitoneum can therefore raise both arterial and end-tidal CO2.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 34, printed p. 809

questions.stem: Lengthening inspiratory time (increasing the I:E ratio) mainly improves what?
options: CO2 clearance from the alveoli each breath
questions.explanation: Lengthening inspiration can increase mean airway pressure and recruit collapsed alveoli, improving oxygenation in selected patients. Shorter expiration also increases the risk of incomplete emptying and auto-PEEP.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 159–160

questions.stem: Which are effects of lengthening inspiratory time? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Note: ↑I → ↑oxygenation but ↓venous return, SV (stroke volume), BP (blood pressure).
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 33

questions.stem: Lengthening expiratory time (decreasing the I:E ratio) mainly improves what?
options: CO2 clearance and less air trapping
questions.explanation: More expiratory time can allow obstructed lungs to empty more fully. When expiration was previously incomplete, this can reduce air trapping and improve effective ventilation.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 644

questions.stem: A COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) patient shows rising peak pressures and expiratory flow that doesn't reach zero. Best I:E change?
options: Keep 1:2 and raise PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) to 15
questions.explanation: Expiratory flow that fails to reach zero suggests incomplete emptying and intrinsic PEEP. Increasing the time for expiration, for example by changing from 1:2 to 1:3, addresses this mechanism.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 644

questions.stem: The default I:E ratio for mechanical ventilation is:
questions.explanation: An I:E ratio of 1:2 is a typical initial adult volume-control setting in the text. It is a starting point that must be adjusted for respiratory mechanics and incomplete expiration.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Which I:E range suits obstructive lung disease?
questions.explanation: At the same respiratory rate, a 1:3–1:4 ratio gives more of each cycle to expiration than 1:2. Longer expiration can help obstructed lungs empty, but the setting must be individualized.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 644

questions.stem: Which I:E range is listed for ARDS (acute respiratory distress syndrome)?
questions.explanation: ARDS can need longer inspiration, up to inverse ratio.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 35

questions.stem: Increasing inspiratory flow rate while keeping RR (respiratory rate) and Vt (tidal volume) constant has what effect?
options: Shortens inspiratory time and lengthens expiratory time
Lengthens both inspiratory and expiratory time
Leaves inspiratory and expiratory time unchanged
Lengthens inspiratory time and shortens expiration
questions.explanation: At fixed tidal volume, increasing constant inspiratory flow delivers the volume in less time. If respiratory rate and pause time are unchanged, the shorter inspiration leaves more time for expiration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 153–154

questions.stem: An inspiratory pause (plateau) is thought to improve what?
questions.explanation: An inspiratory pause holds the delivered volume after flow stops, allowing gas redistribution and keeping alveoli expanded longer. This may reduce shunt and improve oxygenation, while also permitting assessment of static compliance.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 164

questions.stem: The recommended tidal volume is about:
questions.explanation: A protective ventilation strategy can use tidal volumes of 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight. This limits excessive lung stretch; the target is adjusted for the patient and ventilation strategy rather than actual body mass.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 159; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 34, printed pp. 809–810

questions.stem: Tidal volume should be calculated from which weight?
options: Adjusted body weight for all patients
questions.explanation: Tidal volume is based on ideal (predicted) body weight, because lung size follows height rather than total weight. Using actual weight would overinflate the lungs of obese patients.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Set Vt (tidal volume) 500 mL, circuit compliance 4 mL/cmH2O, PIP (peak inspiratory pressure) 25 cmH2O. Using the lecture formula, about what Vt is delivered?
questions.explanation: Assuming zero baseline pressure and no compensation or fresh-gas contribution, circuit volume loss is 4 × 25 = 100 mL. Subtracting this from 500 mL gives approximately 400 mL delivered to the patient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 103; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 152, 165

questions.stem: Circuit compliance stays the same but PIP (peak inspiratory pressure) doubles. How does the volume lost to the circuit change?
questions.explanation: For constant linear circuit compliance, the compliance-related volume change is C × ΔP. Doubling the pressure increment doubles that component of volume loss before compensation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 165

questions.stem: Which are suggested benefits of low tidal volume ventilation? Select 3.
options: Higher EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) at the same rate is desirable
Lower risk of atelectasis without PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure)
Lower mortality in ARDS (acute respiratory distress syndrome)
questions.explanation: Listed benefits; low Vt often needs a higher RR (respiratory rate) and PEEP.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 36

questions.stem: Which trigger method do anesthesia ventilators typically use?
questions.explanation: Note: anesthesia uses flow trigger, usually 2 L/min; flow is most sensitive.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 37

questions.stem: Which trigger type is most sensitive?
questions.explanation: Note: flow is most sensitive.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 37

questions.stem: Trigger sensitivity is set too high (very hard to trigger). What happens?
options: The patient's work of breathing increases
The patient’s work of breathing decreases
PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) is lost from the circuit
questions.explanation: A trigger that is difficult to activate requires the patient to generate more inspiratory effort before assistance begins. The parenthetical definition in the stem matters because numerical sensitivity labels vary between ventilators.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278

questions.stem: Trigger sensitivity is set too low (very easy to trigger). What happens?
options: The patient must work harder to start each breath
The ventilator may trigger without a true patient effort
Triggered breaths fail to be delivered
questions.explanation: If a trigger responds too easily, motion in the surgical field can initiate a breath without a true patient inspiration. Adjusting the trigger threshold or window can reduce this false triggering.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278

questions.stem: A pressure trigger example in the lecture is about:
questions.explanation: Pressure trigger: negative inspiratory pressure, such as −3 cmH2O.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 37

questions.stem: The default PEEP is:
questions.explanation: The lecture's default PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) is 5 cmH2O, titrated to SpO2 (peripheral oxygen saturation) and patient needs. Nurse Anesthesia also cites PEEP of 5 cmH2O with low plateau pressures as lung protective.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 38; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 159

questions.stem: When titrating PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure), the lecture suggests increasing by about:
questions.explanation: Increase about 2 cmH2O every 10–15 minutes to 8–10.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 38

questions.stem: Which are risks of high PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure)? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Note: can ↑ICP (intracranial pressure), hypotension, ↓venous return, barotrauma.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 38

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure)?
options: Shorten expiratory time to clear CO2
Prevent alveolar collapse and improve oxygenation
Increase CO2 elimination from the alveoli
questions.explanation: PEEP helps keep recruitable alveoli open at end expiration, improving oxygenation. Excessive PEEP may overdistend already open alveoli without recruiting additional lung units.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 159, 164

questions.stem: What is the PIP (peak inspiratory pressure) goal in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture goal is PIP under 35–40 cmH2O, with 40 a common default maximum. Nurse Anesthesia Table 16.7 lists PIP under 35, plateau under 28, and driving pressure under 16 cmH2O.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 39; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Ch. 16, printed p. 277 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Per the instructor, a typical PIP (peak inspiratory pressure) for a healthy patient is about:
questions.explanation: Note: normal 13–20; sick or obese about 30.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 39

questions.stem: Which raise PIP (peak inspiratory pressure) by increasing airway resistance? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm, mucus plugging, and biting the endotracheal tube narrow the gas pathway and increase resistance. During volume control, more resistive pressure is needed to deliver the same flow, raising PIP.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 166; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Which raise PIP (peak inspiratory pressure) by decreasing lung compliance? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Pneumoperitoneum, steep Trendelenburg, and atelectatic lung can reduce respiratory-system compliance. At a fixed delivered volume, a stiffer system requires greater inflation pressure.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed pp. 277, 809–810

questions.stem: Which cause PIP (peak inspiratory pressure) to fall? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Bronchodilation reduces resistive load, while release of pneumoperitoneum can improve compliance. A leak or disconnection can also lower measured pressure, so a pressure decrease is not always beneficial.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: PIP (peak inspiratory pressure) suddenly drops from 22 to 8 cmH2O during volume control, and exhaled Vt (tidal volume) falls. FIRST action?
options: Increase PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) by 5 cmH2O
Check for a disconnection or leak
questions.explanation: A sudden decrease in PIP together with a fall in returned tidal volume is consistent with a leak or disconnection. Check the patient, airway, and breathing circuit immediately rather than assuming improved lung mechanics.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Switching from volume control to pressure control usually has what effect on displayed PIP (peak inspiratory pressure)?
questions.explanation: A decelerating flow profile can reduce the early resistive pressure peak. The cited benefit is a lower maximum pressure, not a guaranteed pressure change whenever modes are switched.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 163

questions.stem: During a laparoscopic case, PIP (peak inspiratory pressure) climbs to 38 cmH2O after insufflation. Per the instructor, what is a reasonable step?
options: Ignore it; PIP below 40 is always acceptable
Disconnect the circuit to relieve pressure
Increase tidal volume to recruit lung
Discuss lowering insufflation pressure with the surgeon
questions.explanation: Note: potential for releasing some insufflation; talk to the surgeon.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 39, 41

questions.stem: Plateau pressure is measured when?
questions.explanation: Plateau pressure is assessed during an end-inspiratory pause after airflow has ceased. This removes the pressure contribution from ongoing flow through airway resistance.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 620; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 164

questions.stem: Plateau pressure best reflects what?
options: Airway resistance and ETT (endotracheal tube) size
questions.explanation: During a no-flow inspiratory hold, plateau pressure reflects elastic pressure in the respiratory system together with baseline PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure). It therefore relates more closely to lung and chest-wall compliance than to flow-dependent airway resistance.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed pp. 620–621

questions.stem: Static compliance is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Static compliance is tidal volume divided by plateau pressure minus PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure): Cstat = VT/(Pplat − PEEP). It is assessed under no-flow conditions so the pressure reflects elastic rather than resistive loading.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 620

questions.stem: Dynamic compliance is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Dynamic compliance is VT (tidal volume)/(PIP − PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure)). Because PIP (peak inspiratory pressure) is measured during flow, this value incorporates airway resistance as well as respiratory-system elastic properties.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 621

questions.stem: Vt (tidal volume) 500 mL, Pplat (plateau pressure) 25 cmH2O, PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) 5 cmH2O. Static compliance?
questions.explanation: Static compliance is VT divided by plateau pressure minus PEEP. Here, 500/(25 − 5) = 25 mL/cmH2O.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed pp. 620–621

questions.stem: Vt (tidal volume) 600 mL, PIP (peak inspiratory pressure) 35, Pplat (plateau pressure) 20, PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) 5 cmH2O. Dynamic compliance?
questions.explanation: Dynamic compliance uses peak pressure minus PEEP. Here, 600/(35 − 5) = 20 mL/cmH2O.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 621

questions.stem: Driving pressure equals:
questions.explanation: Driving pressure is plateau pressure minus PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure). It represents the pressure increment used to inflate the respiratory system above the end-expiratory baseline.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Which strategy keeps plateau pressure low to reduce ventilator-induced lung injury?
options: Higher tidal volume with zero PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure)
Lower tidal volume with reasonable PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure)
questions.explanation: Lower tidal volume reduces the elastic pressure needed to inflate the lungs at a given compliance. Appropriate PEEP can limit collapse, but excessive PEEP can increase overdistension and plateau pressure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 159, 164

questions.stem: On this pressure-time waveform, which numbered point is the plateau pressure?
questions.explanation: Point 2 is the plateau reached after inspiratory flow stops. It is used to assess static elastic loading when a valid no-flow hold is obtained.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 620

questions.stem: On this waveform, the difference between points 1 and 2 reflects what?
options: The PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) level set on the vent
A leak in the circuit or cuff
questions.explanation: The difference between peak and plateau pressure is the resistive pressure component during flow. In the passive model, that component equals flow × resistance.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152

questions.stem: On this waveform, which pair of points gives driving pressure?
questions.explanation: Point 2 is plateau pressure and point 3 is baseline PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure). Their difference is driving pressure.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Compared with the gray baseline, which panel shows a resistance problem?
questions.explanation: Panel A shows a higher peak with a similar plateau pressure. At comparable flow and volume, this suggests increased resistance rather than a new elastic load.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152

questions.stem: Which panel shows a compliance problem?
questions.explanation: Panel B raises both peak and plateau pressure. At comparable tidal volume and PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure), that pattern suggests increased elastic loading or reduced compliance.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152

questions.stem: Which panel shows an elevated baseline (PEEP) problem?
questions.explanation: Panel C has an elevated end-expiratory baseline compared with the gray trace. It is consistent with increased PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) and should prompt assessment of both intended and unintended baseline pressure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152

questions.stem: A patient's waveform changes from baseline to panel A. Which is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Panel A raises the peak pressure while leaving the plateau similar. A kinked tube can increase resistance and produce that pattern at comparable flow and volume.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 232

questions.stem: In controlled (mandatory) ventilation, who triggers and cycles the breath?
options: The machine triggers and the patient cycles
The patient triggers and the machine cycles
questions.explanation: In a controlled mandatory breath, the ventilator initiates and terminates the breath according to its settings. Patient effort is not required to start that breath.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 162

questions.stem: In an assisted breath, who triggers and who cycles?
questions.explanation: The patient initiates an assisted volume breath by triggering the ventilator. The machine then delivers and terminates the programmed breath.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168

questions.stem: Controlled modes are necessary for which patients?
options: Patients with an LMA (laryngeal mask airway) breathing spontaneously
Patients with neuromuscular weakness who breathe well
questions.explanation: Apneic or paralyzed patients cannot depend on spontaneous triggering alone. They require a mode capable of delivering mandatory breaths at an adequate backup or controlled rate.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168

questions.stem: In volume control ventilation, which parameter is fixed?
questions.explanation: Volume control targets tidal volume. The pressure needed to deliver it depends on respiratory mechanics and flow, subject to the ventilator’s pressure limits.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 166

questions.stem: In volume control, what happens to PIP (peak inspiratory pressure) when compliance decreases?
options: It drops to PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure)
questions.explanation: Lower compliance requires more elastic pressure for the same tidal volume. Peak pressure therefore rises if flow, PEEP, and delivered volume remain comparable.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 166

questions.stem: Which pairing of mode and main risk matches the lecture?
options: VCV (volume-controlled ventilation) volutrauma; PCV (pressure-controlled ventilation) barotrauma
VCV (volume-controlled ventilation) barotrauma; PCV (pressure-controlled ventilation) volutrauma
questions.explanation: VCV fixes volume so pressure can climb; PCV fixes pressure so volume can swing.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 46, 48

questions.stem: In pressure control ventilation, which parameter is fixed?
questions.explanation: Pressure control targets inspiratory pressure rather than a fixed volume. Flow and tidal volume vary with compliance, resistance, and available inspiratory time.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 166–167

questions.stem: During pressure control, the surgeon releases the pneumoperitoneum. What happens to tidal volume?
questions.explanation: Releasing pneumoperitoneum can improve compliance. At the same pressure target and timing, tidal volume can increase, so volume must be reassessed.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: During pressure control, bronchospasm develops. What happens to tidal volume?
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm increases resistance and can reduce delivered tidal volume during pressure control. A stable pressure setting does not guarantee stable ventilation.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Which inspiratory flow pattern is typical of pressure control?
questions.explanation: Pressure control usually begins with a high pressure gradient and high inspiratory flow. Flow then decelerates as airway and alveolar pressures approach equilibrium.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 166–167

questions.stem: PCV-VG (pressure-controlled ventilation with volume guarantee) adjusts what to maintain the set tidal volume?
options: PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure), over several minutes
questions.explanation: PCV-VG adjusts inspiratory pressure to pursue the selected tidal volume as mechanics change. The adjustment remains constrained by the pressure limit.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278

questions.stem: Why does PCV-VG (pressure-controlled ventilation with volume guarantee) still require vigilance over PIP (peak inspiratory pressure) alarms?
options: It works only during spontaneous breathing
Pressure rises automatically to hold the set Vt (tidal volume)
It can’t change inspiratory pressure at all
It turns off the pressure alarms by design
questions.explanation: The algorithm raises pressure to maintain volume, so pressures can creep up.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 50

questions.stem: What problem with plain PCV does PCV-VG (pressure-controlled ventilation with volume guarantee) address?
options: Inability to set PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) in pressure modes
Lack of a backup rate during apnea
Large Vt (tidal volume) swings with sudden compliance changes
High peak pressures caused by a fixed volume
questions.explanation: Plain pressure control can deliver markedly different volumes when compliance changes. PCV-VG adjusts pressure in response to that variation while retaining a volume target.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278

questions.stem: Which situations favor pressure control? Select 3.
options: Need for a guaranteed fixed volume regardless of compliance
Cuffed ETT (endotracheal tube) with high compliance and no leak concerns
Normal lungs in a short supine case only
questions.explanation: The cited indications include small patients, low-compliance conditions such as laparoscopy, and use with a suitable laryngeal mask airway. Pressure control still requires monitoring because it does not guarantee tidal volume.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed pp. 277–278

questions.stem: Per the instructor, what pressure limit is used with PCV (pressure-controlled ventilation) through an LMA (laryngeal mask airway)?
questions.explanation: Note: LMA doesn't want high pressure; PCV ≤ about 20.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 51

questions.stem: In assist-control ventilation, what does a spontaneous patient-triggered breath receive?
options: Half of the preset tidal volume
Pressure support only, no set volume
questions.explanation: In volume-targeted assist-control, a qualifying patient effort triggers the preset machine tidal volume. The effort does not automatically receive only half of that volume.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168

questions.stem: In assist-control, the patient breathes faster than the set rate. What happens?
options: The ventilator stops assisting those breaths
Controlled breaths are added on top of the assisted ones
Tidal volume is reduced to compensate
No controlled breaths are given; all breaths are assisted
questions.explanation: When accepted patient triggers occur often enough, they satisfy the set control interval and additional untriggered breaths are not needed. The ventilator retains the controlled rate as backup if triggering stops.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168

questions.stem: In SIMV (synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation), what happens if no patient effort is detected within the timing window?
options: The ventilator alarms and stops cycling
No breath is delivered during that interval
A mandatory breath is given at the start of the interval
questions.explanation: In the timing model described in the chapter, lack of a sufficient window signal leads to a mandatory breath at the beginning of the respiratory interval. The implementation should be checked on the actual ventilator.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 169

questions.stem: In SIMV (synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation), effort is detected within the timing window. When is the mandatory breath delivered?
options: It is skipped for that cycle
Immediately after the next spontaneous breath ends
In sync with the effort, at the end of the interval
questions.explanation: The mandatory breath is synchronized with the detected effort.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 54

questions.stem: Which are benefits of SIMV (synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation)? Select 3.
options: Delivers full Vt (tidal volume) with every spontaneous breath
Pressure support available for spontaneous breaths
Eliminates the need for a backup rate
questions.explanation: Note: helps ↓barotrauma, prevents breath stacking.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 56

questions.stem: Why is SIMV (synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation) less likely than assist-control to cause breath stacking?
options: It uses a faster inspiratory flow rate
It delivers smaller mandatory breaths each cycle
It lengthens inspiratory time on each breath
It delivers breaths only when the airway is nearly empty
questions.explanation: Synchronizing breaths to the sensed volume prevents stacking.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 56

questions.stem: What does pressure support do?
options: Adds a preset pressure to patient-triggered breaths
Delivers a fixed volume at a set rate
Holds one continuous pressure throughout the cycle
questions.explanation: Pressure support adds a selected inspiratory pressure to qualifying spontaneous breaths. The resulting volume depends on effort and respiratory mechanics.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168

questions.stem: What does PSV-Pro (pressure support ventilation with apnea backup) add to standard PSV?
options: Backup machine breaths during apnea or failed triggers
Automatic PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) titration to compliance
A higher ceiling on pressure support levels
A guaranteed tidal volume on every single breath
questions.explanation: PSV-Pro adds apnea protection by reverting to backup machine ventilation if spontaneous breathing is not detected. This backup behavior is a specific feature, not inherent to every PSV implementation.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278, 281

questions.stem: The pressure support range listed in the lecture is:
questions.explanation: Goal 5–20 cmH2O.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 57

questions.stem: A pressure-supported breath typically cycles to exhalation when flow falls to about what fraction of peak?
questions.explanation: The illustrated pressure-supported breath cycles off when flow falls to 25% of peak. Actual cycling thresholds are adjustable or device-specific.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168

questions.stem: A patient on PSV (pressure support ventilation) with an LMA (laryngeal mask airway) becomes apneic after an opioid bolus. Which mode prevents a gap in ventilation?
options: Spontaneous mode with the APL (adjustable pressure-limiting valve) open
PSV-Pro (pressure support ventilation with apnea backup)
questions.explanation: PSV-Pro provides backup machine ventilation if spontaneous breaths are not detected. The configured apnea delay and backup settings must still be appropriate.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278, 281

questions.stem: In spontaneous mode, partially closing the APL (adjustable pressure-limiting) valve does what?
options: Adds positive pressure, like PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure)
questions.explanation: Note: spontaneous = open APL; partial closure = some PEEP.
questions.citation: Elmore, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 59

questions.stem: BiPAP (bilevel positive airway pressure) differs from CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) by providing what?
options: A fixed tidal volume with each breath
Two pressure levels, inspiratory and expiratory
questions.explanation: Bilevel support alternates between higher and lower pressure levels. CPAP maintains one continuous baseline pressure without the same pressure cycling.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 279

questions.stem: High-frequency ventilation delivers more than how many breaths per minute?
questions.explanation: The cited technical definition uses a rate exceeding 150 cycles per minute. The same chapter notes that broader descriptions of high-frequency techniques use a wider range.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 170
